summary.title: Demystifying Agent Skills: Why They Work—Until They Don't

setting_and_object.category: Empirical study / Taxonomy (mechanistic analysis of agent skills)

details: Agent "skills" (distilled procedural artifacts such as SKILL.md) are evaluated almost exclusively by aggregate task success, leaving unexplained when they help, why they work, and where they fail.
Skill design is therefore heuristic: no account of what changes in agent behavior once a skill is loaded, or which pipeline stage (representation, retrieval, invocation, adaptation) breaks.

A contrastive paired-trajectory analysis methodology: for each task, matched executions under three arms (Raw, Workflow Memory, Skill) built from the *same* source trajectories are compared, with an LLM judge assigning a mode to each arm and recording what the treatment fixed vs. introduced, plus a mechanism label (procedural anchor / knowledge injection / failure warning / none / counterproductive).

The resulting artifact: a taxonomy of skill use with 3 high-level skill-use categories and 12 fine-grained modes, induced bottom-up by open coding rather than imposed, used to attribute gains and failures to concrete mechanisms instead of success rates.
Three arms: Raw (no prior experience), Workflow Memory (cleaned procedural traces), Skill (same workflows distilled into a standardized SKILL.md placed in the execution environment).
Fixed-budget composition grid over source trajectories: 5s0f through 0s5f (successful/failed mixtures) per task, with balanced pools collected per task.
RQ2 no-hint ablation: identical trajectories but success/failure annotations hidden from the skill creator.
RQ3 transfer: artifacts built from Codex trajectories evaluated in Gemini CLI against its own Raw baseline.

Agent-model pairings: Codex + GPT-5.3-Codex and Gemini CLI + Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview (RQ1-RQ3); Codex + GPT-5.4 and Gemini CLI for RQ4 selection/execution; Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B for embedding retrieval.
Benchmarks: Terminal-Bench 2.0 (89 tasks), Terminal-Bench-Pro (200-task public split), SkillsBench (86 tasks, 11 domains, with native ground-truth task-skill annotations).
Harbor evaluation workflow, n=5 trials per task, parallelism 20; Terminal-Bench-Pro conditions use 130 trials with infrastructure errors counted as failures.

8,135 normalized trial records (7,837 with transcripts); stratified open coding of 240 sampled trajectories by Claude Sonnet 4.6 with tools/session disabled and fixed head/tail transcript budgets; 238 valid unique labels.
Two-round batched induction (batches of ~60, 8-14 modes per batch, merged to 9-14) yielding 12 canonical modes; success/failure taken from verifier reward, not agent self-report.
528 paired triples (SkillsBench 144, TB2 186, TB-Pro 198) = 1,584 arm-level assignments; deterministic representative-trial selection and 1,000-iteration bootstrap CIs.
Human validation: 714 trajectory-label grounding checks and independent re-mapping of all 238 labels to the 12 modes.
Candidate pools contain the task's ground-truth skills plus distractors; pool size k in {5,10,20,50,100}; distractor regimes random, embedding-similar, and dissimilar.

Three independent arms, with no outputs passed between them: Arm 1 embedding top-1 ranking, Arm 2 explicit agent selection without execution, Arm 3 full-pool real execution with post-hoc parsing of which skills were inspected/invoked.
Metrics: per-record precision/recall over canonical skill IDs, F1 recomputed from aggregated P and R, plus binary verifier success.
Lightweight compact-procedure baselines on 26 Terminal-Bench-2 tasks (130 trials): instruction-derived short plan and workflow-derived test-first template, injected as plain text.
Matched token-cost analysis on the 83-task intersection where Raw, Workflow Memory, and Skill all have complete token metadata.

key_findings.finding: Skills help mainly by procedural anchoring (stabilizing action) rather than by injecting missing factual knowledge, and their clearest advantage is over workflow memory built from identical trajectories.
key_findings.evidence: Across 528 paired triples, oracle success is 61.9% (Skill), 59.1% (Raw), 55.9% (Workflow Memory); the only paired delta with a CI excluding zero is Skill vs Workflow Memory, +6.06 pp [+0.76, +11.36]. Mechanism labels assign procedural_anchor to 65.7% of skill cases versus 4.5% for knowledge_injection. Compact-text baselines (short plan 47.7%, test-first template 59.2%) fall below Workflow Memory (62.3%) and far below Skill (79.2%) on 26 TB2 tasks, so compact procedural text alone does not explain the gain.

key_findings.finding: Skills systematically reduce execution-layer failures but do nothing for failures requiring problem reformulation or true runtime verification, and they introduce a new invocation/applicability failure surface.
key_findings.evidence: SC2 execution-layer failures fall from 37.3% (Raw) and 33.3% (Workflow) to 23.5% (Skill), with environment_infrastructure_failure 5.3%->1.7%->0.2%, output_format_schema_mismatch 7.4%->3.2%, service-lifecycle 2.7%->0.8%. In contrast algorithmic_logic_error (8.3/11.0/7.4%) and static_verification_without_runtime (12.5/12.5/11.7%) are essentially unchanged, while skill_guidance_misapplied_or_ignored rises to 10.0% in skill arms versus 0.8% raw and 0.4% workflow; SC3 totals 78/528 for Skill vs 19/528 for Raw.

key_findings.finding: Retrieval is a separate bottleneck: as skill pools grow, agents almost stop restricting use to the correct skill, yet downstream success barely changes, so exact ground-truth invocation is neither sufficient nor necessary.
key_findings.evidence: In Arm 3 on SkillsBench, averaged actual-use precision drops from 29.6% (k=5) to 3.3% (k=100) while success moves only 36.4%->39.3% (Gemini 16.9%->0.7% precision with flat 36-39% success; Codex 42.3%->5.9% precision with success rising 35.4%->42.0%); Arm 3 recall remains 54.3-73.6% at k=100, indicating agents inspect the right skill among many distractors.

key_findings.finding: Semantic confusability, not pool size, is the dominant stressor for offline skill identification, and offline identification quality is decoupled from downstream execution.
key_findings.evidence: Arm 1 top-1 precision falls 70.5%->53.4% (k=5->100) on similar pools versus 97.7%->84.1% (random) and 96.6%->93.2% (dissimilar); Arm 2 explicit selection on similar pools is 54.3% (Gemini) and 51.9% (Codex) at k=5 and 55.4%/31.9% at k=100, while average selection recall stays 70.5-85.2% at k=100 and Arm 3 success stays near 36-42% across all regimes.

key_findings.finding: Explicit success/failure annotations matter chiefly when the source pool contains failed trajectories, and skills trade extra context for effectiveness relative to workflow memory.
key_findings.evidence: No-hint skill creation is near-parity at 5s0f but degrades as failures enter the pool, e.g. Gemini on Terminal-Bench-2 at 3s2f: 0.7462 (normal) vs 0.4000 (no-hint), with the same pattern across completed Gemini TB2/SkillsBench ratios. On the matched 83-task intersection, Workflow Memory is cheapest (426.2K total tokens, 64.8% success) while Skill reaches 69.6% at 521.5K tokens, still below Raw's 555.7K.
